covers.quote: Use the right name
Use the form the person uses.
As far as possible, if you need to write a non-English name, use the same form and spelling as the person uses.

rules.quote: When you write to or about people, always use the form of personal name that the person uses.
rules.specification: Use the personal name, spelling, and styling preferred by the individual.
rules.violation_condition: using a form of a personal name other than the one used or preferred by the individual
when: A few people deliberately do not use capitals for their names (for example, bell hooks, kd lang).
rules.why: G-1, G-2, G-4: Core instruction on respecting the preferred name/form across generic, uncapitalised, and non-English names.

covers.quote: ‘given name’ instead of ‘Christian name’
‘family name’ instead of ‘surname’
‘previous names’ instead of ‘maiden name’.

rules.quote:
To avoid cultural or gender bias when referring to parts of names, use:

‘given name’ instead of ‘Christian name’
‘family name’ instead of ‘surname’
‘previous names’ instead of ‘maiden name’.
rules.specification: Substitute 'given name' for 'Christian name', 'family name' for 'surname', and 'previous names' for 'maiden name'.
rules.violation_condition: using 'Christian name', 'surname', or 'maiden name' when referring to parts of personal names
rules.why: E-3, G-2: Lead-in and list items specify preferred neutral terminology over biased terms.

covers.quote: Use initial capitals for personal names, initials and nicknames

examples.note: Capitalised personal name

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for the names of real and fictitious people.
rules.violation_condition: writing the personal name of a real or fictitious person without initial capitals
when: Exception for people who deliberately do not use capitals for their names (for example, bell hooks and kd lang).
rules.why: G-1: Heading is broken down into specific rules for names, initials, and nicknames.

examples.note: Unspaced initial without full stop
Middle initial without full stop
Multiple initials unspaced and without full stops
Hyphenated initials retaining individual's name form

rules.quote: Capitalise the initials of people’s given names. Write them unspaced and without full stops. Use non-breaking spaces to ensure that initials are not separated from family names.
rules.violation_condition: given name initials written in lower case, with spaces between initials, with full stops, or separated from the family name by a breaking space
rules.why: G-2: Covers capitalisation, spacing, lack of full stops, and non-breaking space for personal initials.

examples.note: Nickname in quotes with initial capitals
Nickname in quotes with initial capital
Nickname in quotes with initial capitals
Nickname in quotes with initial capital
Nickname in quotes with initial capitals

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for nicknames. The first time they appear in your text, place nicknames in quotation marks.
rules.violation_condition: a nickname written without initial capitals, or appearing for the first time without quotation marks
when: Quotation marks are only required the first time the nickname appears in the text.
rules.why: G-2: Covers both initial capitalisation and first-instance quotation mark requirements for nicknames.

covers.quote: Spell plural forms correctly

examples.note: Plural of names ending in s, z, x

parts.quote: There were 3 Yanises and 2 Lizes at the meeting but no Alexes.

examples.note: Plural of name ending in y keeps y and adds s

parts.quote: The Murphys always meet on Tuesdays.

examples.note: Plural of name ending in i keeps i and adds s
Plural of name ending in o adds s

parts.quote: The 4 young Angelos played together all day.

examples.note: Plural of name ending in other letters adds s

parts.quote: The 2 Evelyns in the section were cousins.

rules.quote: The plural of any personal name is formed by adding ‘s’ or ‘es’.
rules.specification: Add 'es' for names ending in 's', 'x', and 'z'. For all other endings (including 'y', 'i', 'o'), keep the final letter and add 's'. Never use an apostrophe to form a plural.
rules.violation_condition: forming the plural of a personal name by using an apostrophe, changing the ending (e.g. changing 'y' to 'ies'), or using an incorrect suffix
rules.why: G-1, G-2: Table 1 elaborates the exact suffix rules ('es' vs 's') governed by this rule statement.

covers.quote: Punctuate possessive forms with an apostrophe

examples.note: Singular name ending in s takes apostrophe s
Singular name ending in another letter takes apostrophe s

rules.quote: Use an apostrophe and an ‘s’ with personal names, even when they already end in ‘s’ (Table 2).
rules.violation_condition: a singular personal name in the possessive case written with only an apostrophe instead of an apostrophe and 's'
when: Applies to singular personal names.
rules.why: G-1: Distinct rule for singular possessives, requiring 's even after 's'.

examples.note: Plural name takes only an apostrophe

parts.quote: The Joneses’ responses or the Nasrins’ name tags

rules.quote: Plural personal names take just an apostrophe. Simply add an apostrophe to the end of the plural form.
rules.violation_condition: a plural personal name in the possessive case written with an apostrophe and an extra 's'
when: Applies to plural personal names.
rules.why: G-2: Contrasting rule to singular possessives.

covers.quote: Keep hyphens and all parts of compound family names

examples.note: Retaining hyphen in compound family name
Retaining hyphen in compound given name

rules.quote: Always retain hyphens when you write given and family names that are hyphenated.
rules.violation_condition: omitting a hyphen from a hyphenated given or family name
rules.why: G-1: Heading covers both hyphens and compound parts; each has distinct rules.

covers.quote: Sometimes someone has more than one family name but is only known by one. Write all the names the first time and use the well-known family name after.

examples.note: Delafield Cook is retained as compound family name
All names written first time even though artist is known as Allport

rules.quote: Write all parts of compound family names. Keep the compound when writing a person’s family name.
rules.violation_condition: dropping or omitting part of a compound family name, unless the person is only known by one family name after first mention
when: If someone has more than one family name but is only known by one, write all names the first time and use the well-known family name thereafter.
rules.why: G-2: The exception for well-known single names is folded into the compound names rule under When.

covers.quote: Keep accents and diacritic marks in names

examples.note: Accented name
Diacritics retained
Umlaut retained

rules.quote: When you write names, retain diacritic marks unless the person commonly uses a simplified form of their name.
rules.violation_condition: omitting diacritic marks from a personal name when the person does not commonly use a simplified form
when: Does not apply if the person commonly uses a simplified form of their name.
rules.why: G-1, G-4: Mark the operative instruction with its explicit exception.

covers.quote: Treat names with particles case by case

examples.note: Lower case particle
Lower case particles
Upper case particle
Capitalised particle
Capitalised particle

rules.quote: Use the same capitalisation as the person uses. It is largely a matter of individual preference and family custom. If you can’t ask them, use reliable resources to decide on a case-by-case basis, then use the same form throughout the content.
rules.specification: Follow the person's casing for name particles (e.g. van, de la, Van, Du). Keep usage consistent throughout the document.
rules.violation_condition: capitalising a name particle inconsistently or contrary to the person's established usage
when: Always use an initial capital for the particle when the name starts a sentence.
rules.why: G-1, G-2: Covers treatment and consistency of particles.

examples.note: Particle capitalised at start of sentence

parts.quote: Van Otterloo was chief conductor of the Sydney Symphony Orchestra.

examples.note: Sentence rephrased to retain lower case particle

parts.quote: The chief conductor of the Sydney Symphony Orchestra was van Otterloo.

rules.quote: Always use an initial capital for the particle when a name starts a sentence. You can also rephrase the sentence to retain the original form.
rules.violation_condition: beginning a sentence with a lower case particle in a personal name
when: Applies when the name appears at the very beginning of a sentence.
rules.why: G-2: Specific mandatory capitalisation requirement for sentence-initial particles.

covers.quote: List family name first in reference lists

rules.quote: In a reference list, put the family name first and then the initial for the given name of the lead author.
rules.violation_condition: listing given names or placing given initials before the family name for the lead author in a reference list
when: Applies to author names in reference lists.
rules.why: G-1, G-4: Specific format instruction for author names in reference lists.

examples.note: Names pronounced 'Mac' ordered as if spelt the same way

rules.quote: Names you pronounce the same way but spell differently go together in an alphabetical list.
rules.specification: Group identically pronounced family name prefixes (such as Mac, Mc, M') as if spelt the same way.
rules.violation_condition: alphabetising phonetically identical family names strictly by their literal spelling rather than grouping them together (e.g. separating MacArthur, M'Cay, McFarlane)
when: Applies when sorting alphabetical lists of names.
rules.why: G-2, E-3: Specific rule for alphabetical sorting of phonetically identical names.
